1408.title: Your family
1408.howItsDone: Muslim families may pray some prayers together at home, with one person leading and the others standing behind in a row and children joining as they learn, following the hadith that encourages praying some prayers in the house.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your character, one trait at a time, and a nightly ledger called muhasabah. Your line was one trait.

A man named al-Aswad put a plain question to Aisha: what did the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, do at home? Not in the mosque, not leading anyone. At home. Her answer, in Sahih al-Bukhari: he would be busy serving his family, and when the time for prayer came, he would go out to pray. That's the whole report. No miracle in it. A man helping around the house, then stopping for prayer. A strangely ordinary thing to have been remembered.
screen: `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `SERVING HIS FAMILY.` → `THEN, THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: That report sets the order of things. Service at home and prayer aren't rivals; the same person does both, in the same afternoon. Then the house itself. In another hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet tells his followers to pray some of their prayers in their houses, and not to make their houses like graves. The picture is stark: a house with no prayer in it is likened to a grave. Praying together: one can lead and the others stand behind in a row. A parent leads, a child stands beside or behind, and the prayer is said at the same pace. Small children wander in and out of it. In Bukhari there's a report of the Prophet praying while carrying his little granddaughter Umamah, setting her down when he went down in prostration and picking her up when he stood. The tradition didn't wait for a quiet house to pray in one. And families as they really are. Some homes are all Muslim. Some have a new Muslim and parents who aren't. Some have a spouse from another faith or none. Praying together can mean one person praying while another sits nearby in quiet, or a family sharing a meal and saying bismillah before it. In surah Ta Ha, Allah tells the Prophet to bid his household to prayer and to be patient in it. Patient is the word to keep. Habits at home grow slowly, and nobody is helped by being pushed.
screen: `SERVICE AT HOME, THEN PRAYER.` · `DON'T MAKE YOUR HOUSE A GRAVE.` · `ONE LEADS, A CHILD BESIDE.` · `FAMILIES AS THEY REALLY ARE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you live with, or the family you're closest to, one face at a time, and let one small act of service come to mind for one of them: a dish washed, a bag carried, a phone call returned. If you pray, choose one prayer today and invite someone at home to stand with you for it, simply, without a speech; if you or your family don't pray, one quiet moment shared at a meal is enough.
Your family. The first place practice is lived: serving at home, and praying there too. Today's word.
Your line: pray together. Service first, then the prayer, in the same afternoon. See you tomorrow.

1409.title: Your neighbor
1409.hook: faith lived beside neighbors of every kind
1409.howItsDone: Muslims treat the neighbor's rights as part of faith, following the Qur'an's command to be kind to the near and the stranger neighbor and the hadith 'let him honor his neighbor'; this can mean sharing food on holidays, avoiding noise and harm, and checking on neighbors of any faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your family, service at home, then the prayer, and patience above all. Your line was pray together.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once told his companions: Jibril kept urging me to treat the neighbor well, so often that I thought he was going to make the neighbor an heir. That report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. An heir. Someone with a share in what is yours, written into the family accounts. The person whose music comes through the wall, whose car blocks yours, whose name you might not even know. You met the neighbor back on day one hundred fifty-four. Today, faith lived beside neighbors of every kind.
screen: `JIBRIL KEPT URGING.` → `AS IF THE NEIGHBOR WERE AN HEIR.` → `THE ONE THROUGH THE WALL.`

segments.voice: In surah an-Nisa, in a list of those to be treated with kindness, after parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, the Qur'an names the neighbor who is related to you, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side. Two kinds of neighbor in one verse: one who shares your family, and one who shares nothing with you but a fence. The bar is set high. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor. And in the same collection, that a person whose neighbor isn't safe from his harm will not enter paradise. So a neighbor isn't a matter of manners. It sits right next to faith itself. Neighbors of every kind, too. A report in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi tells of the companion Abdullah ibn Amr, who had a sheep slaughtered at home and asked his household: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor? Then he repeated the hadith of Jibril and the neighbor. The neighbor's faith didn't change the neighbor's right. On an ordinary street it starts small. Knowing a name. Not letting your trash cans block a driveway. Keeping the noise down at night. A plate of food over the fence on a holiday, any holiday. Checking on the older man upstairs when it snows. Rights like these are small, and they're owed whether or not the neighbor returns them.
screen: `THE NEAR NEIGHBOR AND THE STRANGER.` · `HONOR YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `HAVE YOU GIVEN SOME NEXT DOOR?` · `SMALL RIGHTS, OWED ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: In your mind, step out your front door and look left, right, up or down, silently naming every neighbor whose name you know, and notice where the names run out. Pick one door where you don't know a name, and let one small, easy reason to knock come to mind: an introduction, a plate of something, a question about the building. If you pray, ask Allah to bless the people on your street.
Your neighbor. The person on the other side of the wall, whose rights the Qur'an and the Prophet set right next to faith. Today's word.
Your line: start next door. A name is where it begins. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1410.title: Your service
1410.howItsDone: Muslims serve others through food pantries, hospital visits, mosque kitchens and community volunteering, describing it as khidmah, service, and as worship when done for Allah's sake; a hadith says that whoever visits the sick will find Allah there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your neighbor, the near one and the stranger, and rights owed either way. Your line was start next door.

Son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says Allah will speak words like these on the Day of Resurrection. The person is bewildered: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And the answer comes: My servant so-and-so was sick, and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. The same exchange follows about food and about water. A hospital room, a hungry stranger, a thirsty one. Khidmah.
screen: `I WAS SICK.` → `HOW COULD I VISIT YOU?` → `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Khidmah is service, the work of looking after someone else's needs. In Muslim communities you'll hear it for everything from serving tea at a gathering to running a food pantry. Why does service count as worship? That hadith does something bold. It doesn't put service next to worship. It puts Allah inside the visit. Nobody in the story is praying, and yet the sick room is where Allah is found. How is it meant to be done? In surah al-Insan, the Qur'an describes people who give food, for love of Him, to the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and who say: we feed you only for the sake of Allah; we want no reward from you and no thanks. That's a high bar, and an honest one. Service that waits for applause starts to become about the server. The same hour at a shelter can be a chore, a line on an application, or worship. The givers in al-Insan say theirs out loud: for the sake of Allah. What changes is what the hour is for. And the promise. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says Allah is in the help of His servant as long as the servant is in the help of his brother. So service isn't only something given away. In the tradition's telling, the one who serves is also being served.
screen: `KHIDMAH: LOOKING AFTER NEEDS.` · `ALLAH FOUND IN THE SICK ROOM.` · `NO REWARD, NO THANKS.` · `HELPED WHILE HELPING.`

segments.voice: Let your breath go out a little longer than it comes in, and bring to mind someone who is sick, or alone, or short of something this week, someone real if you can, without trying to fix anything yet. Let the hadith's question land: if you visited, what would you find there? If you pray, make your intention for Allah; if you don't, simply set your intention to show up without needing thanks.
Khidmah. Service to people, given for Allah's sake, without waiting for reward or thanks. Today's word.
Your line: serve. No applause needed, because the hour was never about the server. Until tomorrow.

1411.title: Your balance
1411.hook: worship, work, rest and family: give each its right (Bukhari)
1411.howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of Salman and Abu al-Darda, 'give each one its right', as a guide to balancing worship, work, rest and family, so that devotion does not crowd out sleep, health or the rights of a spouse and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khidmah, the sick room where Allah is found, and no thanks needed. Your line was serve.

Salman comes to visit his friend Abu al-Darda and finds Abu al-Darda's wife in shabby, careless clothes. What's wrong? he asks. Your brother, she says, has no interest in this world. Abu al-Darda puts food in front of his guest and says: eat, I'm fasting. Salman says: I won't eat unless you eat. So he eats. That night Abu al-Darda gets up to pray, and Salman tells him: sleep. Later he gets up again. Sleep, says Salman. Near the end of the night, Salman wakes him, and the two of them pray together. Then Salman says the line Sahih al-Bukhari keeps.
screen: `A WIFE IN SHABBY CLOTHES.` → `EAT. SLEEP.` → `THEN THEY PRAY TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Your Lord has a right over you, your own self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give each one its right. When they told the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, what had happened, he said: Salman has spoken the truth. Notice who was out of balance. Not a lazy man. A devout one, fasting through the day and rising to pray through the night, while his wife sat in shabby clothes. Too much of a good thing had pushed something else out. Another report in Bukhari tells it a second way. The Prophet hears that the companion Abdullah ibn Amr fasts every day and prays every night, and tells him: fast and break your fast, pray and sleep, for your body has a right over you, your eyes have a right over you, and your wife has a right over you. Eyes have a right. Sleep isn't a lapse in devotion. It's owed. Why it holds together: the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." A practice that breaks the person practicing it isn't what was asked. These weeks you've met a diverse ummah, asked the questions of today, and built a practice for today, one piece at a time. Balance is what keeps all of it standing. Not everything every day. Each thing its right.
screen: `GIVE EACH ONE ITS RIGHT.` · `A DEVOUT MAN, OUT OF BALANCE.` · `YOUR EYES HAVE A RIGHT.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: Go through the four rights one at a time and give each a breath: worship, where it has a place in your day; work, what it asked of you today; family, one face, one need; and yourself, your body, your eyes, how tired they are. Notice which one got crowded out this week, no blame, just notice. If you pray, thank Allah for the day in your own words.
Your balance. Giving your Lord, yourself, your family and your work each their right, so none crowds out the rest. Today's word.
Your line: give each its right. This block ends here, and the year starts gathering itself in. Rest well tonight.

1412.title: The pillars, reviewed
1412.hook: five pillars, now understood from the inside
1412.howItsDone: Muslims keep the pillars as acts with set forms: saying the testimony, praying the daily prayers at their times, paying zakat on qualifying wealth, fasting the month of Ramadan, and making the Hajj if able; teachers stress the intention and humility behind each act.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your balance, Salman's line, and each thing its right. Your line was give each its right.

Five words fit on an index card: testimony, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage. A visitor to a mosque could learn the list over one cup of tea. You met them on day nine, as a house built on five. This year stayed a long while inside each one: the words of the testimony, the standing and bowing of the prayer, the arithmetic and the mercy of zakat, the long afternoons of the fast, the white cloth of the pilgrimage. Now the year is closing, and these last days gather what it taught. First, the pillars, from the inside.
screen: `FIVE WORDS ON AN INDEX CARD.` → `A LONG WHILE INSIDE EACH ONE.` → `NOW, FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says Islam is built on five: bearing witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger, establishing the prayer, giving zakat, the pilgrimage, and fasting Ramadan. Built on: a house, not a checklist. Now each one from the inside. The testimony is said with the tongue, and Muslim teachers say it has to be meant: words that count when they're sincere. The prayer: the Qur'an praises the believers "Who are humble in their prayers." Standing and bowing are the outside; that humility, khushu', is the inside. Zakat: the Qur'an tells the Prophet to take alms from people's wealth to purify them, in paraphrase. The giving cleans the giver, not only feeds the poor. The fast: in Pickthall's Qur'an, fasting is prescribed "that ye may ward off (evil)." The hunger is the outside; the guarding is the inside. The pilgrimage: the Qur'an says the flesh and blood of the sacrifice don't reach Allah, but the devotion of the people does, in paraphrase. Each pillar has a body and a heart. In Muslim teaching, the body is required: the movements, the amounts, the days. And the texts keep pointing past the body to what it carries. Not skipping the outside, but finding what it holds. And the pillars lean on each other. The prayer holds the day. The fast holds a month. The pilgrimage, for whoever is able, can hold a whole life.
screen: `BUILT ON FIVE: A HOUSE, NOT A LIST.` · `EACH PILLAR HAS A BODY AND A HEART.` · `HUMBLE IN PRAYER, GUARDED IN THE FAST.` · `THE PILLARS LEAN ON EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next prayer of the day, the one coming after this lesson. If you pray, decide now where you'll be when it comes, and plan to stop for it when it arrives, not after. If you don't, choose that same moment anyway, and when it comes, pause for one breath and remember that somewhere, someone is standing for that prayer just then.
The pillars. The five things Islam is built on, in the hadith's words: testimony, prayer, zakat, pilgrimage and fasting, each with a body and a heart. Today's word.
Your line: from the inside. The body of each pillar carries a heart. Until tomorrow.

1413.title: The reports, reviewed
1413.howItsDone: Muslims read hadith in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and Shia Muslims in their own collections such as al-Kafi; scholars grade each report by its chain and its text, and teachers often give the source and grade when they quote one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pillars, each with a body and a heart. Your line was from the inside.

A message lands in a family group chat late at night. It begins, the Prophet said, then a beautiful sentence, then a row of heart emojis. Somebody's aunt has already forwarded it to her other groups. Nobody asks where it came from. This year spent a long stretch on exactly that question. Before a sentence could be called a hadith, scholars wanted to know who said it, who heard it, who passed it on, and whether every one of those people could be trusted. Today, how a hadith reaches you.
screen: `THE PROPHET SAID… FORWARDED.` → `WHERE DID IT COME FROM?` → `HOW A HADITH REACHES YOU.`

segments.voice: A hadith is a report of what the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, did, or approved. Every hadith has two halves: a chain, the isnad, and a text, the matn. The chain is the list of people: I heard it from this one, who heard it from that one, all the way back. Why did the chain matter so much? In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, a saying is recorded from the early scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, in paraphrase: the chain is part of the religion, and without it anyone could say whatever they liked. The forwarded message problem, named long before phones. How was it tested? Scholars wrote about the narrators themselves, the science the year called rijal: was this man truthful, was his memory sharp, did he really meet the one he quoted? They tested the text too, asking whether it fit the Qur'an and the known sunnah. Then they graded: sahih, sound; hasan, good; da'if, weak; and some reports were exposed as fabricated. And the people who carried it. Students traveled to hear a report from its source, and memorized chains by heart. Women carried it too, from Aisha onward, and the year met Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih. The same introduction to Sahih Muslim carries a warning, in paraphrase: it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything they hear. That sentence could sit above every share button.
screen: `A CHAIN AND A TEXT.` · `WITHOUT THE CHAIN, ANYONE SAYS ANYTHING.` · `TESTED, THEN GRADED.` · `CARRIED BY MEMORY AND TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hadith you met this year whose source you actually know: actions are by intentions, from Bukhari, or none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself, also Bukhari. Hold its words for a few breaths, and think of one person who might be glad to hear it, with its source attached, the way the scholars would have wanted.
The reports. Hadith: what the Prophet said, did, or approved, each carried by a chain of named people and tested before it was trusted. Today's word.
Your line: the chain holds. It holds because people checked it, link by link. See you tomorrow.

1414.title: The schools, reviewed
1414.howItsDone: A Muslim may follow one school of law, learned from family, a mosque or a teacher, and Muslims of different schools pray side by side in the same congregation, each following their own school's details.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the reports, a chain and a text, tested before trusted. Your line was the chain holds.

A caliph, tradition says, once came to Imam Malik of Medina with an offer. Malik had gathered his book of reports and rulings, the Muwatta. The caliph wanted copies sent to every province, with orders that everyone follow it and nothing else. One book, one law, no more arguments. Malik turned him down. The companions of the Prophet, he said, had spread out to many lands, and the people in each place had already heard reports and acted on them. Let them keep what they have.
screen: `ONE BOOK FOR EVERY PROVINCE?` → `MALIK SAID NO.` → `WHY MORE THAN ONE SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Start with the path and the map. Shari'ah is the path Allah set. Fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it, human work, done with care. A school, a madhhab, is a tradition of that understanding, carried from teacher to student. Every school begins with the Qur'an, then the sunnah. Sunni schools add the agreement of scholars and reasoning by likeness. Ja'fari jurists, followed by Twelver Shia, count reason itself as a source alongside the Qur'an, the sunnah and consensus. The year walked through the names one by one: Hanafi, from Abu Hanifa in Kufa; Maliki, from Malik in Medina; Shafi'i; Hanbali, from Ahmad ibn Hanbal in Baghdad; Ja'fari, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq; Zaydi, in Yemen; Ibadi, in Oman; and Zahiri, the school of the plain sense. A statement of scholars called the Amman Message named these eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers. Why do they differ? Scholars received different reports, read words in different ways, weighed methods differently, and all of them were seeking the same thing: what Allah asks. A saying the year met calls that difference a mercy; some attribute it to early scholars rather than to the Prophet. So when one person in a prayer row folds his hands high and the next folds them low, neither is a mistake waiting to be fixed. Each is a school's careful answer, the kind Malik chose to leave in place.
screen: `THE PATH, AND THE SCHOLARS' MAP.` · `THE SAME SOURCES, WEIGHED DIFFERENTLY.` · `HANAFI TO ZAHIRI: EIGHT NAMED.` · `DIFFERENT ANSWERS, ONE DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: Bring back Malik's answer, let them keep what they have, and let it settle. If you pray at a mosque this week, you can stand next to someone whose prayer looks different from yours and simply pray, without a word about it afterward. If you don't pray, think of one person whose practice differs from yours in a small way, and let it be their careful answer, not a mistake.
The schools. Traditions of fiqh, human understanding of the divine law, each built from the same sources and each still standing in the same row. Today's word.
Your line: many schools, one row. Shoulder to shoulder, facing one direction. Same time tomorrow.
